title: Dynamic range, intermodulation, link budget
blurb: Explain dynamic range and intermodulation, find third-order products, read intercept points, and work a dB link budget.

E4D01.why: Blocking dynamic range = the dB span from the **noise floor** up to the level causing **1 dB of gain compression**.
E4D01.trap: The IMD-products definition is a different measure; intercept point isn't the end of the window.

E4D02.why: A receiver that can't handle strong signals shows **cross modulation and desensitization** from strong adjacent signals.
E4D02.trap: Oscillator drift and LO injection are not dynamic-range problems.

E4D03.why: Two nearby transmitters' outputs **mix in the final amplifier**, a nonlinear stage, creating products.
E4D03.trap: Feedback and harmonic relationships aren't what mixes them.

E4D04.why: A **terminated circulator** at the transmitter output is a one-way valve: the nearby signal can't reach the final amplifier.
E4D04.trap: A band-pass filter or Class C or D amplifier doesn't stop the other signal mixing in.

E4D05.trap: Check each pair: 2f₁ − f₂ or 2f₂ − f₁ must equal the receive frequency.

E4D06.why: A strong nearby signal reducing sensitivity is **desensitization**.
E4D06.trap: Cross modulation moves the strong signal's modulation onto yours; reciprocal mixing comes from oscillator noise.

E4D07.why: **Attenuation before the first RF stage** lowers the strong signal so it can't overload the receiver.
E4D07.trap: More front-end gain makes overload worse.

E4D08.why: Intermodulation needs a **nonlinear** circuit or device, so signals can mix with each other.
E4D08.trap: Feedback and neutralization affect stability, not mixing.

E4D09.why: A preselector is a tunable filter ahead of the first stage that **rejects signals outside the band** being received.
E4D09.trap: It filters; it doesn't store frequencies or attenuate broadband.

E4D10.why: At the **intercept point**, a pair of 40 dBm tones would give a third-order product **equal in amplitude to either tone**.
E4D10.trap: It's a theoretical extension of the lines, not a noise-floor or audibility limit.

E4D11.why: Odd-order products of two in-band signals fall **close to them**, so also in band. Even-order ones fall far away.

E4D12.trap: Subtracting MDS alone ignores the required S/N.

E4D13.trap: Both antennas' gains count: don't leave out the receive antenna.

E4D14.trap: Each −10 dB divides power by 10; −100 dB is ten steps below 1 mW.
